passage:
"Ritu didi, Raghunath is the best batsman in the world. Ever."
"He got out for two yesterday, Samir."
"That was the umpire. It wasn't even out."
"And last week, zero?"
"The pitch was bad. Everyone got out."
"The other team's captain made eighty on the same pitch."
"He got lucky. Raghunath made a hundred in March. Remember? Remember the six over the stand?"
"That was March. It's August."
"So? He's still the best."
Ritu pulled up the scores on Papa's phone. "Look. Six matches, and he crossed thirty once."
Samir glanced at the screen and pushed it away. "Those numbers are wrong. You don't understand cricket."
He went back to his poster of Raghunath and smoothed the corner that had curled.

qa.q: How many runs did Raghunath score yesterday?
qa.a: He got out for two.

qa.q: Why does Samir keep explaining away Raghunath's low scores?
qa.a: Samir feels loyal and proud of his hero, so remembering the big hundred feels right, and the bad scores feel unfair rather than true.

qa.q: What could help Samir see the scores more fairly?
qa.a: He could write down every score for a month, good and bad, and look at the whole list with Ritu before deciding.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Samir's loyalty?
qa.a: Ritu seems amused and a little frustrated, trying to show him the numbers while he pushes them away.

grounding: It shows a boy who insists his favourite cricketer is the best, remembers only the matches that prove it, and blames bad scores on the umpire or pitch.

passage: Last summer, I was sure Lalthanga, the Mizoram team opener, was the best batsman ever. I had his photo inside my pencil box. When he scored fifty, I told everyone at school. When he got out early, I said the bowler was cheating or the umpire was blind. My friend Lalremsiami kept a notebook of scores. One day she showed me: in ten matches, he'd scored fifty only twice. I said her notebook was wrong. I got really angry. At home, Papa said, "Amandeep puttar, you remember the fifties because you love him." I didn't want to hear it. Now I think Papa was a bit right. I still like Lalthanga. But I also look at the whole notebook.

qa.q: How many times did Lalthanga score fifty in ten matches?
qa.a: Only twice.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep get angry when Lalremsiami showed the notebook?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defensive, because loving his hero made the good scores feel like the whole truth, so the notebook felt like an attack.

qa.q: What does Amandeep do differently now?
qa.a: He still likes Lalthanga but looks at the whole notebook, good and bad scores, before deciding who is best.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when Amandeep said her notebook was wrong?
qa.a: Lalremsiami may have felt annoyed or hurt, since she had kept careful records.

grounding: It shows a boy who believed his favourite cricketer was the best and remembered only the good matches, explaining away bad scores.

passage:
Class 5 note, Friday

During the cricket discussion today, Pradeep told the class his favourite player "never fails." When Vikram mentioned the player's low scores in the last series, Pradeep said, "The umpires were against him. And it rained." When another child mentioned a century, Pradeep lit up and described every shot.

It was clear he only remembered the matches that fit. The rest were bad luck.

I didn't correct him in front of everyone. After class I asked him to fill in a small table from the newspaper: every score in the last ten matches. He was unhappy at first. When he finished, he looked at it for a long time and said, "Maybe he's the best sometimes."

I'll use the same table idea for our maths lesson on averages next week.

— Vidya

qa.q: What did Pradeep say when Vikram mentioned the low scores?
qa.a: "The umpires were against him. And it rained."

qa.q: Why did Pradeep light up at the mention of a century?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, because the century fit his belief about his hero, so it was the kind of fact he wanted to hear.

qa.q: What was wise about Vidya's table idea?
qa.a: It made Pradeep look at all the scores himself, privately, so he could see the pattern without feeling embarrassed in class.

qa.q: How might Vikram have felt when Pradeep blamed the umpires?
qa.a: Vikram may have felt frustrated or brushed off, since his fact was dismissed.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a boy who insists his favourite cricketer never fails and remembers only the matches that prove it.

passage: Sarita, you think Anjali in your class is fake? Let me tell you about your Pranav mama and a boy called Rakesh, when I was fifteen. I decided in the first week of Class 10 that Rakesh was a show-off who only pretended to be nice. After that, every message he sent in the group chat, I read like a detective. If he wrote "congrats!" to someone, I thought, fake. If he shared notes, I thought, he wants attention. When he sent me a birthday wish, I didn't even open it. My feed showed me only what I clicked on, and I clicked on the posts that made him look silly. By March I was sure I was right. Then I got chicken pox and missed two weeks. Rakesh was the only one who came to my house with all the notes. I still remember his face at the door.

qa.q: What did Rakesh bring to Pranav's house?
qa.a: All the notes.

qa.q: Why did reading Rakesh's messages 'like a detective' feel reasonable to young Pranav?
qa.a: Having decided early that Rakesh was fake, Pranav felt sure and a little proud of seeing through him, so every message seemed to prove it.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Pranav have tested the belief?
qa.a: When Rakesh sent the birthday wish, opening it and reading it fairly would have been a chance to check whether the belief was true.

qa.q: How might Rakesh have felt when his birthday wish was ignored?
qa.a: Rakesh may have felt hurt and confused, trying to be friendly without knowing why it wasn't returned.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a teenager, Pranav decided a classmate was fake and read every message as proof, skipping anything friendly.

passage: It was exam week, and Thomas's phone had only a little data left for the month. He should have saved it for the online practice papers. Instead, he spent it scrolling the class group chat, looking for proof that Jatin was fake. Thomas had decided it after Jatin was chosen class monitor. Now every message looked like evidence. Jatin's "good luck all 👍" was a show. Jatin's shared formula sheet was just to look helpful in front of the teacher. When Jatin wrote "anyone need help with chapter 4?" Thomas scrolled past without reading the replies, which were mostly thank-yous. His feed kept showing him posts that made Jatin look like a try-hard, because those were the ones he opened. On Thursday his data ran out. He still hadn't opened the practice paper.

qa.q: What did Jatin share in the group chat?
qa.a: A formula sheet.

qa.q: Why did every message from Jatin feel like proof to Thomas?
qa.a: Thomas felt resentful after Jatin became monitor, and having already decided Jatin was fake, each message seemed to confirm it, which felt satisfying.

qa.q: What could Thomas do to test the belief?
qa.a: He could read Jatin's messages and the replies fully for a day and note anything friendly, not just what fits his view.

qa.q: How might the classmates who thanked Jatin see him?
qa.a: They seem to see Jatin as helpful and kind, very different from how Thomas sees him.

grounding: It shows a teenager who has decided a classmate is fake and reads every message for proof, skipping friendly ones, while the feed serves what fits.

passage: In their Pune flat, Uday lay on his bed scrolling the Class 11 group chat. Ever since Sarika laughed when he dropped his tiffin in the canteen, he'd been sure she was fake, nice to teachers and mean behind their backs. Now he searched her messages. "Great job, everyone!" — fake. "Sorry I missed practice" — making excuses. He screenshotted the ones that sounded rude and sent them to his friend with an eye-roll emoji. When she messaged the whole group, "Uday, hope your hand's better after the match!", he didn't reply. He told himself she only wrote it because the teacher was in the group. His mother called him for dinner. He kept scrolling, thumb moving fast past anything friendly, stopping only when something fitted.

qa.q: What did Sarika do in the canteen that started Uday's belief?
qa.a: She laughed when he dropped his tiffin.

qa.q: Why does ignoring Sarika's friendly message feel reasonable to Uday?
qa.a: Uday feels hurt and embarrassed from the canteen moment, so a friendly message doesn't fit his view and he explains it away as fake.

qa.q: What could Uday try to see Sarika more fairly?
qa.a: He could list all her messages, friendly and not, and ask whether she laughed at the tiffin or at something else before deciding.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel when Uday doesn't reply?
qa.a: Sarika may feel ignored or puzzled, not knowing he thinks she's fake.

grounding: It shows a teenager who has decided a classmate is fake and searches only for proof while skipping friendly messages.

passage:
Week one, a Monday. Pradeep decided in the hostel mess: he would skip campus placements and prepare for a design career. That night he searched "why placements are overrated" and read five articles. All agreed with him. He felt thorough.

Week two, a Thursday. Farida, a senior who had done both, told him, "Sit for placements anyway. You can say no later." Pradeep nodded and forgot it by dinner. He messaged two seniors who had skipped placements and were happy. Their replies he saved in a folder called 'Research.'

Week four, a Friday. The placement registration closed. Pradeep's folder had fourteen articles and six messages, all saying the same thing. Farida's advice wasn't in it. When a friend asked if he'd looked at the other side, Pradeep said, "I did a lot of research," and meant it.

qa.q: What did Pradeep name the folder where he saved replies?
qa.a: 'Research.'

qa.q: Why did Pradeep feel thorough even though he only read agreeing sources?
qa.a: He felt confident and well researched because the folder was full, but he had searched in a way that only found agreement, so it felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Pradeep have done to test his decision?
qa.a: He could have searched for the best arguments for placements and saved Farida's advice in the same folder before deciding.

qa.q: How might Farida feel when she learns Pradeep skipped placements?
qa.a: Farida may feel disappointed and a little frustrated that her advice was forgotten.

grounding: It shows a student who collects only articles and seniors' advice that back skipping placements, feeling well researched while gathering agreement, over several weeks.

passage: Suraj, you want to skip placements? Before you decide, let me tell you what I did at twenty-one. I'd already decided I would skip placements and study for an MBA abroad. Then I "researched." I read only blogs by people who had done exactly that. I asked only the two seniors I knew had loved it. When my professor said, "Payal, the job market might be tight next year; keep one offer in hand," I smiled and thought he didn't understand. I felt so well informed. My notebook was full of quotes. Then the admissions came back: two rejections and a waitlist. And no job offer, because I hadn't sat for any. I spent a year at home. I wasn't stupid. I just collected agreement and called it research.

qa.q: What did Payal's professor advise?
qa.a: "The job market might be tight next year; keep one offer in hand."

qa.q: Why did young Payal feel so well informed?
qa.a: Payal felt confident because the notebook was full of quotes, not noticing that every quote agreed with the decision already made.

qa.q: What turning point in the story could have changed the outcome?
qa.a: If Payal had taken the professor's advice seriously and sat for placements as a back-up, there would have been an offer in hand after the rejections.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt seeing Payal's choice?
qa.a: The professor may have felt worried and a bit frustrated, knowing the risks.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a student, Payal gathered only sources that agreed with skipping placements and felt well researched.

passage: The gap-year application form was due tomorrow at noon, and the hostel Wi-Fi was down, so Yamini sat in the cyber café near the college gate with one hour of paid time. She had already decided: she'd take a year off after second year to travel and work. Now she was building her case. She opened blog after blog titled "Best decision of my life." She skipped a long article called "What nobody tells you about gap years" without clicking. Her friend Vinita had messaged: "Have you asked the dean's office about losing your hostel seat?" Yamini read it and put the phone face down. At minute fifty-five, she printed the form. She felt thorough, a little proud. Walking back, she realised she hadn't read a single thing that disagreed with her.

qa.q: Where did Yamini go because the hostel Wi-Fi was down?
qa.a: The cyber café near the college gate.

qa.q: Why did Yamini feel thorough and proud walking back?
qa.a: She felt confident because she had read many blogs, but they all agreed with a decision already made, so collecting them felt like research.

qa.q: What could Yamini do before submitting the form?
qa.a: She could read the 'What nobody tells you' article and ask the dean's office about her hostel seat, as Vinita suggested.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel seeing her message ignored?
qa.a: Vinita may feel worried and a bit brushed off, having raised a real concern.

grounding: It shows a student who picks only sources backing a decision already made, feeling well researched while only collecting agreement.

passage:
Floor mentor's log, Block B, Tuesday

My roommate Karthik has been talking about his food-delivery app idea for three weeks. Every time someone encourages him, he quotes them for days. "Priya said it's genius." When the professor in the entrepreneurship class said the market was crowded, he said the professor was outdated. When a senior asked about costs, he changed the subject.

I've felt uneasy watching this. Arguing each point hadn't worked; he just defended harder.

Tonight I tried something different. I said, "Karthik, I've noticed you remember every yes and forget every no. Can we write down the no's too, just to see them?" He was quiet, then a bit hurt. But he wrote them. Three pages of yes, one page of no. He looked at it for a long time.

Will check in on Thursday.

— Kashish

qa.q: What did the professor say about the app idea?
qa.a: The market was crowded.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel watching Karthik dismiss the warnings?
qa.a: Kashish felt uneasy and a bit helpless, since arguing point by point only made Karthik defend harder.

qa.q: Why did naming the pattern work better than arguing?
qa.a: It described what Karthik was doing without attacking the idea, so he could look at the no's himself instead of defending.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel looking at the page of no's?
qa.a: Karthik may feel hurt and uncertain, but also more aware of warnings he had skipped.

grounding: It shows a roommate noticing a friend dismiss every warning about a shaky startup idea while quoting praise, and kindly naming the pattern.

passage:
Wednesday

Gopika has quit her part-time job to start a home tiffin service from our flat. I'm her flatmate, so I've watched it all. When her aunt praised her biryani, Gopika quoted it for a week. When the man at the next building said three tiffin services had already closed on our street, she said he was jealous. When I asked about the kitchen space, she said, "Varun, don't be negative."

I tried arguing about costs. It went badly. She stopped talking to me for a day.

Tonight, over chai, I tried something softer. "I think you hear the yes's louder than the no's. That's human. Can we list both?" She was annoyed at first. Then she laughed a little and said, "Maybe."

I really want this to work for her. That's why I said it.

Varun

qa.q: What did the man at the next building say?
qa.a: That three tiffin services had already closed on their street.

qa.q: How does Varun feel about Gopika's plan?
qa.a: Varun feels worried but caring, wanting the plan to work, which is why the concerns were raised gently.

qa.q: What made Varun's second approach better than the first?
qa.a: Naming the pattern kindly, 'you hear the yes's louder', instead of arguing about costs, let Gopika consider it without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How does Gopika seem to respond to the gentle approach?
qa.a: Gopika is annoyed at first, then laughs a little and says 'maybe', showing she's starting to consider it.

grounding: It shows a flatmate who notices a friend dismissing every warning about a shaky business idea and gently names the pattern instead of arguing point by point.

passage:
Thursday

New colleague Chandrika started on Monday. First day she was ten minutes late. I knew right then: not serious.

Tuesday she asked where the printer was. Obviously didn't read the onboarding doc. Wednesday she sent an email to the wrong client list, only two people, but still.

Today in the team meeting, Sir praised the pricing model she built. Honestly, I think someone helped her. Or it was a template.

I told Arun at lunch that she's weak and he'll see. He said her pricing model was actually clever. I said one good thing doesn't cancel three mistakes.

Walking home, I tried to remember something bad she did today. Couldn't. Still, I know my type.

— Leela

qa.q: How late was Chandrika on her first day?
qa.a: Ten minutes late.

qa.q: Why does Leela feel sure Chandrika is weak?
qa.a: Leela felt certain from the first late arrival, so each slip felt like proof and the good pricing model felt suspicious, which makes the judgement feel reasonable.

qa.q: What could Leela do to check the first impression?
qa.a: Leela could list everything Chandrika did this week, good and bad, and ask whether the late arrival would matter if the pricing model came first.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel if she sensed Leela's judgement?
qa.a: Chandrika might feel unwelcome and anxious in her first week, not knowing why.

grounding: It shows a young professional who decides early that a new colleague is weak and reads each slip as proof while dismissing her good work.

passage: At the small cooperative bank branch in Kalimpong, the new clerk, Maria, arrived in the cold December rain with a dripping umbrella and tracked mud across the floor. Tenzin, the assistant manager, sighed. Careless. After that he noticed everything. Maria stamped a form on the wrong page. Careless. She asked a customer to repeat his account number. Slow. When she stayed late to reconcile the cash register perfectly, Tenzin assumed the senior clerk had done most of it. When an elderly farmer came in specially to thank Maria for explaining his loan papers in Nepali, Tenzin was at lunch and heard about it later. "She's nice to old people," he said. "Doesn't make her good at the job." In the quarterly review, he rated her 'needs improvement.' The senior clerk read it and frowned.

qa.q: What did the elderly farmer thank Maria for?
qa.a: Explaining his loan papers in Nepali.

qa.q: Why did each small slip feel like proof to Tenzin?
qa.a: After the muddy first day, Tenzin felt sure Maria was careless, so every slip seemed to confirm it and the good work felt like someone else's, which felt reasonable to him.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do before the next review?
qa.a: He could note Maria's work every day for a month, including the cash reconciliation and the farmer's thanks, and ask the senior clerk for input.

qa.a: The senior clerk seems to disagree, frowning, likely knowing Maria's good work firsthand.

passage: The dairy cooperative in Anand was about to switch cattle-feed suppliers, and Disha, the young manager, was sure the new supplier was better. It was cheaper and the samples looked good. But before signing, during the Holi holidays when the office was half empty, she sat down and wrote a question in her notebook: what would change my mind? She wrote: if the milk yield drops in the trial, if the farmers complain, if the supplier missed deliveries elsewhere. Then she called Vishal, the oldest vet in the district, who she knew disliked new suppliers. "Tell me every reason this is a bad idea." He talked for twenty minutes. Two points stung. She didn't argue. She wrote them down. Then she asked the supplier for a two-month trial with ten farmers first. Vishal grunted. "Sensible."

qa.q: Who did Disha call before signing?
qa.a: Vishal, the oldest vet in the district.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when two of Vishal's points stung?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable but stayed curious instead of defensive, writing them down rather than arguing.

qa.q: Which of Disha's steps made her decision stronger?
qa.a: Writing what would change her mind, asking a smart critic for the best case against, and running a trial before committing.

qa.q: How does Vishal seem to see Disha's approach?
qa.a: Vishal seems grudgingly impressed, calling the trial sensible even though he dislikes new suppliers.

grounding: It shows a mature worker who asks what would change her mind, seeks a critic and hears the case against before committing.

passage: In the architecture office in Istanbul, the week before the spring holidays, Dalia had a design she loved: a glass atrium for the new library. Everyone on her team liked it. That worried her. Before the client meeting, she wrote on a sticky note: 'What would make me drop this?' Then she walked over to Elif, the engineer known for tearing designs apart. "Please give me the strongest case against the atrium." Elif raised her eyebrows, then listed: summer heat, cleaning costs, glare on reading tables. Dalia's cheeks went warm. It hurt a little. But she thanked Elif, and that evening she read two reports on glass buildings in hot climates. The next day, she presented a smaller atrium with shaded panels. The client asked about heat. Dalia already had the answer.

qa.q: What did Dalia write on the sticky note?
qa.a: 'What would make me drop this?'

qa.q: How did Dalia feel when Elif listed problems with the atrium?
qa.a: Dalia's cheeks went warm and it hurt a little, but she felt grateful and treated the criticism as useful information.

qa.q: Why did seeking Elif's criticism help Dalia?
qa.a: Hearing the best case against let her fix real problems before the client meeting, turning disagreement into data.

qa.q: How might Elif feel being asked to critique on purpose?
qa.a: Elif seems surprised and perhaps pleased to be valued for honest critique.

grounding: It shows a mature worker who asks what would change her mind, seeks a sharp critic and reads the case against before committing.

passage: The school staff room was decorated for Christmas, paper stars hanging from the fan, when Rehana, the new head of the science department, proposed ending the weekly unit tests. She had read three studies that supported her. But she had also learned to distrust how good that felt. At the meeting, she said, "Before we decide, I'd like to hear the best case for keeping the tests." She turned to Simran, the maths teacher who had argued with her all year. "You'll do this better than anyone." Simran blinked, then spoke for ten minutes: parents rely on the marks, weaker students need regular practice, teachers catch gaps early. Rehana wrote each point down. Afterwards she changed her proposal: monthly tests instead of weekly, with short quizzes in between. Simran said, "I can live with that."

qa.q: What did Rehana propose ending?
qa.a: The weekly unit tests.

qa.q: Why did Rehana distrust how good the supporting studies felt?
qa.a: She knew agreement can feel reassuring even when it's one-sided, so she felt cautious and wanted to hear the other side.

qa.q: What did Rehana's choice to ask Simran achieve?
qa.a: It brought out strong reasons she had missed and led to a better compromise that both could accept.

qa.q: How might Simran feel being asked for the best case?
qa.a: Simran seems surprised and perhaps respected for the first time in a year of arguments.

grounding: It shows a mature worker who seeks a smart critic and hears the best case against her proposal before committing, treating disagreement as data.

passage:
Monday. At school in Bhopal, an older boy offered Wasim a sheet of shiny dinosaur stickers. "Fifty rupees." Wasim gasped. Fifty was a lot. He only had twenty in his pocket.

Wednesday. Wasim asked his sister Sunaina for money. "He'll give it for thirty now! I bargained!" He was so proud. Twenty whole rupees less! Sunaina frowned. "Thirty for one sheet of stickers?" "It was fifty!" Wasim said. She gave him ten, still frowning.

Saturday. At the stationery shop near the market, Wasim saw the same dinosaur stickers on a hook. The price tag said ten rupees. He stared. He counted on his fingers. He had paid thirty. He felt his face go hot. "But he said fifty," he whispered to Sunaina. She put an arm around him. "That's why he said fifty first."

qa.q: How much did the stickers cost at the stationery shop?
qa.a: Ten rupees.

qa.q: Why did Wasim feel proud paying thirty rupees?
qa.a: The first price of fifty stuck in his mind, so thirty felt like a big win, even though it was still too high.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time someone names a price?
qa.a: He could check the price in a shop first, or ask Sunaina, before deciding if a deal is fair.

qa.q: How does Sunaina seem to feel when Wasim sees the ten-rupee tag?
qa.a: Sunaina seems sympathetic and gentle, putting an arm around him instead of saying 'I told you so'.

grounding: It shows a child who treats the first price he hears as the fair baseline, so a lower but still high price feels like a win, over several days.

passage: Elizabeth, you want to know why I always ask the price in three shops? Let me tell you about the Lepcha stall at the Darjeeling mela when I was ten. A man had these beautiful glass marbles, blue with white swirls. I asked, "How much?" He said, "Thirty rupees for five." That was huge then. I bargained, and he came down to twenty. I felt like the cleverest girl in the hills. I ran to show my Ama. She looked at the marbles and laughed. "Dolma, the shop by the monastery sells ten for ten rupees." I didn't believe her. We walked there. She was right. I cried the whole way home. It wasn't the money. It was that I had felt so clever. The first number had tricked me into thinking twenty was cheap.

qa.q: What did the man first say the marbles cost?
qa.a: Thirty rupees for five.

qa.q: Why did young Dolma feel so clever after bargaining to twenty?
qa.a: The first price of thirty made twenty feel like a big win, so Dolma felt proud even though the marbles were still overpriced.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Dolma have avoided being tricked?
qa.a: Before bargaining, she could have checked other stalls like the shop by the monastery to know what a fair price was.

qa.q: How might Dolma's Ama have felt when her daughter cried on the way home?
qa.a: Ama may have felt tender and a bit sorry, knowing the lesson hurt but would stay with her.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, the first price she heard made a still-high price feel like a win.

passage: The school fair in Jaipur closed at five, and Disha, nine, had only ten minutes left and forty rupees from Papa. At the last stall, a big girl was selling sticker books. "Eighty rupees." Disha's heart sank. "Please, I only have forty." The girl sighed dramatically. "Okay, okay. Fifty." Disha begged. "Forty-five, final." Disha ran to borrow five rupees from her friend Raghav, who was eating candyfloss. "Quick! She came down from eighty!" Raghav handed over five. Disha bought the book, grinning. "I saved thirty-five rupees!" she told everyone. On the way home, Raghav flipped through it. "It says twenty on the back," he said, pointing to the printed price. Disha looked. Twenty. She had felt so clever. Now she felt her cheeks burn.

qa.q: What price was printed on the back of the sticker book?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: Why did Disha feel she had saved thirty-five rupees?
qa.a: The first price of eighty stuck in her mind, so forty-five felt like a huge discount and she felt clever, even though it was more than double the printed price.

qa.q: What could Disha try next time at a stall?
qa.a: She could look for a printed price or ask a friend what things usually cost before bargaining from the seller's number.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel pointing out the printed price?
qa.a: Raghav might feel a little awkward, not wanting to upset Disha but thinking she should know.

grounding: It shows a child who treats the first price as the fair baseline, so a lower number feels like a big win even when it's still too high.

passage: In Singapore, Xin's first maths test of the year came back with 90. His mother put it on the fridge. Three weeks later, the second test: 70. He walked home slowly, feeling sick. Seventy felt like failing. At the bus stop, his friend Mateo was grinning. "Seventy! Last time I got fifty!" Mateo held up his paper like a trophy. Xin looked at the same number on his own paper and couldn't understand how it could make Mateo so happy. At home he hid the test in his bag. When his mother asked, he said, "Not good." She looked. "Seventy is a good mark, Xin." "It's twenty less than before," he said, and went to his room. He lay on his bed, the 90 on the fridge still in his head.

qa.q: What did Xin score on the second test?
Why did seventy feel like failing to Xin?
qa.a: His first score of 90 became his yardstick, so seventy felt like a drop, and he felt ashamed and sick, even though it's a good mark.

qa.q: What could help Xin see his mark more fairly?
qa.a: He could look at what he got wrong and how seventy compares with the class, instead of only comparing with the first 90.

qa.q: How does Mateo experience the same mark?
qa.a: Mateo feels proud and happy, because seventy is a big jump from his first score of fifty.

grounding: It shows a teenager who feels terrible about 70 after a first test of 90, while 70 pleases a friend whose first score was 50.

passage: At the residential school in Dehradun, results were pinned on the notice board outside the dining hall. In the first term, Siddharth had got 88 in physics. Everyone congratulated him. This term, 72. He stood in front of the board and felt his stomach drop. Preeti, from the next section, squeezed in beside him. "Seventy-two! Finally!" Her first-term mark had been 55. She was almost dancing. Siddharth tried to smile. At lunch, he pushed his rice around. His housemaster noticed. "Seventy-two is solid, Siddharth." "It's sixteen marks less." "Less than what?" "Than before." The housemaster was quiet for a moment. "If this had been your first mark, how would you feel?" Siddharth thought. "Okay, I suppose." He was still upset. But something in the question stayed with him.

qa.q: What did Siddharth get in physics in the first term?
Why did Siddharth feel his stomach drop at 72?
qa.a: His first mark of 88 set the standard, so 72 felt like a loss, making him feel disappointed even though it's a solid mark.

qa.q: How does the housemaster's question help Siddharth?
qa.a: Asking how he'd feel if 72 were his first mark helps him see that the first result is setting the yardstick.

qa.q: How does Preeti feel about her 72?
qa.a: Preeti is thrilled, almost dancing, because her first-term mark was 55.

grounding: It shows a teenager who feels bad about a second mark because his first higher mark became the yardstick.

passage:
Dear Afreen,

You asked about my results. Honestly, I'm a bit down. First unit test in chemistry, I got 92. I was so happy, Ammi made kheer and called me her clever son. Second unit test: 74.

I know 74 isn't bad. My friend who got 51 last time got 74 too, and he was jumping around the corridor. His whole family is celebrating.

But for me, it just feels like I fell. Every time I look at 74, I see 92 next to it.

I keep asking myself what went wrong, but I studied just as much. Maybe the test was harder? I didn't even check the class average. I just felt bad.

Anyway, how are your exams going? Write back soon.

Vijay

qa.q: What did Vijay get in the first chemistry unit test?
Why does Vijay feel down about 74?
qa.a: The first score of 92 is his yardstick, so 74 feels like falling, making him feel disappointed even though a friend celebrates the same mark.

qa.q: What could Vijay check to see his mark more fairly?
qa.a: He could check the class average and whether the test was harder, instead of only comparing with his first score.

qa.q: How might Afreen respond to Vijay's letter?
qa.a: Afreen might feel sympathetic but also want to remind Vijay that 74 is good and the first score isn't the only measure.

grounding: It shows a teenager who feels down about 74 because his first result of 92 became the yardstick, while a friend celebrates the same mark.

passage: Ritu, you're looking for a flat? Listen, let me tell you about my first one, after college in Bengaluru. The landlord said, "Twenty-five thousand a month." My heart jumped. I'd thought maybe fifteen. But I didn't know the area, and that twenty-five just sat in my head. I bargained. He came down to twenty-two. I felt like I'd won something. I signed that evening. A month later, my colleague moved into a same-size flat two streets away. Fifteen. She'd looked at ten flats first. I'd looked at one. I kept thinking: why did twenty-two feel cheap? Because I started from twenty-five. His number, not mine. So please, look at many flats before anyone tells you a price. That's Ganga's lesson.

qa.q: What did the landlord first ask for the flat?
qa.a: Twenty-five thousand a month.

qa.q: Why did twenty-two feel like a win to Ganga?
qa.a: The landlord's first number stuck, so twenty-two felt cheap and Ganga felt pleased, even though similar flats cost much less.

qa.q: What could Ritu do differently when flat-hunting?
qa.a: Ritu could look at many flats and compare prices before hearing any landlord's number, so Ritu's own research sets the baseline.

qa.q: How might Ganga's colleague have felt, having looked at ten flats first?
qa.a: The colleague probably felt confident and calm about the price, knowing what the area actually charged.

grounding: It shows a graduate who heard the first quoted rent and adjusted too little from it, so the arbitrary figure pulled the final price toward itself.

passage:
May, a Monday. Lakshmi's first job offer arrived by email: a trainee role at a logistics company in Chennai, with a salary figure she'd never imagined. She read it three times. It felt enormous.

The following Thursday. The HR person called. "Any questions on the offer?" Lakshmi had read that you should always ask for more. She asked for a little above their figure, not much. They agreed immediately. She hung up, thrilled. Her friend Jasleen asked, "Did you check what others get?" "No, but I negotiated!"

July, a Friday. At the induction, Lakshmi sat with other trainees. Over lunch, two of them mentioned their pay. Both were noticeably higher. They had researched typical trainee salaries and started from those numbers. Lakshmi had started from the company's. She put down her fork. "I thought I'd done well," she said quietly.

qa.q: Where was Lakshmi's trainee role?
qa.a: At a logistics company in Chennai.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi feel thrilled after the call?
qa.a: The company's first figure felt so big that asking for a little more felt like a win, so she felt proud and excited.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi have done before the call?
qa.a: She could have researched typical trainee salaries or asked seniors or a careers adviser, so her starting point wasn't only the company's number.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel learning what happened?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel sympathetic, having asked about checking what others got.

grounding: It shows a graduate who adjusts too little from the first salary offer, letting the opening figure pull the final agreement toward itself, over several weeks.

passage: Elizabeth, you've got your first offer letter? Wonderful. Sit, I'll tell you what happened with mine, in Delhi, when I was a young woman of twenty-two. The company offered a figure. Before that, I had no idea what a fair salary was. So their number became my world. I asked for a tiny bit more, felt brave, and signed. Two years later, my manager showed me the salary survey for our role. I was well below the middle. Not because I was worse. Because I'd started from their number and moved a few steps. My friend Sudha, who joined the same month, had asked a senior first, and she started from the survey. We did the same job. So before you reply to them, talk to people in the field and the college careers office. That's what Parul learned the hard way.

qa.q: Who showed Parul the salary survey?
qa.a: Her manager, two years later.

qa.q: How did young Parul feel after asking for a tiny bit more?
qa.a: Parul felt brave and satisfied, because the company's number had become the only reference, so a small increase felt like a win.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference between Parul and Sudha?
qa.a: Sudha asked a senior and started from the salary survey, while Parul started from the company's number and moved only a little.

qa.q: How might Sudha have seen the offer when she joined?
qa.a: Sudha likely felt more confident and informed, knowing what the role usually paid before she replied.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how the first salary offer pulled her final agreement toward itself because she adjusted too little from it.

passage: Sabina, you're about to negotiate your first contract? Let me tell you about the day I learned about first numbers. I was twenty-four, a young man working as a junior buyer at a textile firm in Surat. My boss, Mr Kapadia, went to buy cotton from a big supplier, and I sat in. The supplier spoke first. "Ninety a kilo." Mr Kapadia had been thinking seventy. But after that, every offer circled ninety. Eighty-five. Eighty-two. They settled at eighty. I watched Mr Kapadia's face afterwards; he looked uneasy. I felt uneasy too, like I'd watched a trick. So the next time I negotiated, I prepared my own range from the market reports before the meeting. When the supplier said ninety, I said, "Our research says sixty-five to seventy-two," and worked from that. That's how Farhan stopped being pulled.

qa.q: What price did the supplier first say?
qa.a: Ninety a kilo.

qa.q: How did young Farhan feel watching the negotiation?
qa.a: Farhan felt uneasy, as if he had watched a trick, seeing how the supplier's first number pulled every offer toward it.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Farhan in later negotiations?
qa.a: He prepared his own range from market reports before meetings, so he reasoned from research rather than the supplier's first figure.

qa.q: How might Mr Kapadia have felt after settling at eighty?
qa.a: Mr Kapadia seemed uneasy, perhaps realising he had moved far from his own seventy.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how he noticed the first number shaping a negotiation and began preparing his own range from research.

passage: The video call with the printing vendor kept freezing, and Darshan could only hear every second word. His colleague Manjula was leading the talk for the event brochures. The vendor spoke first: "For five thousand copies, two lakh." The screen froze on his smile. When it came back, Manjula was already saying, "Could you do one lakh eighty?" Darshan felt his stomach tighten. Last month he had seen the same thing: whoever named the first figure, the whole talk stayed near it. And Manjula hadn't checked other quotes. He quickly typed in the chat to her: "Our three quotes last year were 1.2 to 1.4." She read it, paused, and said, "Actually, the market rate we've seen is closer to 1.3." The vendor went quiet. The connection dropped again. Darshan made a note: next time, get the range ready before the call.

qa.q: What did the vendor first quote for five thousand copies?
qa.a: Two lakh.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when Manjula offered one lakh eighty?
qa.a: Darshan felt his stomach tighten, worried because he'd seen how the first figure pulls the whole talk toward it.

qa.q: What could Darshan and Manjula do before the next call?
qa.a: They could gather quotes and prepare a range in advance, so they reason from research instead of the vendor's number.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel after using Darshan's message?
qa.a: Manjula may feel relieved and grateful, and perhaps more aware of how quickly she followed the vendor's number.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing that the first figure shapes a negotiation and preparing a researched range to reason from instead.

passage: In the conference room of the software firm in Gurugram, Chinmay watched his colleague Dhruv negotiate with a new client. The client said, "We were thinking of paying thirty lakhs for the project." Dhruv had planned to ask for fifty. But now Dhruv started at thirty-eight. The client came up to thirty-five. They shook hands. Chinmay noticed something that bothered him: the whole talk had stayed close to thirty, the first number said. Afterwards, in the corridor, Dhruv said, "Not bad, right? Five above their offer." Chinmay didn't want to spoil his mood, but he felt uneasy. That weekend, he pulled out the rates from their last ten projects and wrote down a range. The next month, before his own client meeting, he said the range first, calmly, and explained where it came from.

qa.q: What did the client say they were thinking of paying?
qa.a: Thirty lakhs for the project.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay feel uneasy in the corridor?
qa.a: Chinmay noticed the whole talk stayed near the client's first number, even though Dhruv had planned fifty, and felt uneasy that Dhruv didn't see it.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do to avoid the same trap?
qa.a: He researched rates from past projects, wrote down a range, and stated it first in his own meeting with the reasons behind it.

qa.q: How does Dhruv seem to see the deal?
qa.a: Dhruv seems pleased, thinking five above the client's offer was a good result, not noticing the first figure pulled it down.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing that whoever names the first figure shapes the talk, and preparing his own researched range beforehand.
